drafted_from: tool:check-a-servers-tls-owner-on-the-server's row in tools/renew-a-tls-certificate/tool-rows.json, do-work/renew-a-tls-certificate.mjs, do-work/tls-host-owner.py and the tests in test/
start_here: Say to your AI: "Run the certificate owner's own tests on my server at 192.0.2.34, signing in as admin." It runs tool:check-a-servers-tls-owner-on-the-server, which puts the test file beside the owner and runs it there.
no_lists_because: It keeps no list of its own: it takes one server's facts as its input and answers what that server's certificate owner reports.
instructions: 1. Gather the server's facts: its public name, IPv4 address, SSH port, the administrator you sign in as, its pinned key ("<address> ssh-ed25519 <key>") and its layout (host: owner path, state folder, downloads folder, ingress, receptionist). The README in tools/renew-a-tls-certificate/ shows a made-up one.

2. Say to your AI the sentence in start_here. It calls run_resource_operation at @workshop-tools with method tools:run, tool tool:check-a-servers-tls-owner-on-the-server and that input (the worked example shows one). The door mounts your server administration key for the run; you paste no key.

3. Read what comes back: {"host_tests": "passed"} (or the test output when it printed any). An {"error": ...} or a thrown message names what to change (for example the layout or the pinned key was refused).

4. A failure comes back as an error naming the process status; the Linux-only checks (the DNS key in an anonymous memory file, a failed provider never returning the key, a dry run asking staging) only run here.

worked_examples.title: Run the Linux-only owner tests on the server
worked_examples.ask: Test the certificate owner on my server.
worked_examples.given: Read from tools/renew-a-tls-certificate/do-work/renew-a-tls-certificate.mjs (host-test copies test/tls-host-owner.test.py to host.owner with .test.py and runs it with /usr/bin/python3; unittest writes to stderr, so a pass leaves stdout empty and the answer is passed).
